claims.text: Whether CrFeCoNiX forms and retains a stable, coherent oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by whether the alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy in a single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloy produces a random and homogeneous distribution of metal cations.
A homogeneous cation distribution promotes formation of a slow-growing oxide scale.
A homogeneous cation distribution promotes formation of a chemically inert oxide scale.
The oxide formed on a homogeneous single-phase alloy is closely lattice-matched to the alloy substrate.
Close oxide–substrate lattice matching lowers mismatch strain and interfacial stress.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiAl or CrFeCoNiSi can form protective Al2O3 or SiO2 layers, respectively.
The protective scales formed on single-phase alloys can accommodate thermal expansion.
Phase boundaries in multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys act as stress concentrators.
Multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys exhibit compositional segregation at phase boundaries.
Phase-boundary segregation causes localized variations in oxide-growth kinetics.
Multiphase regions produce local differences in thermal-expansion coefficients.
Variations in oxide-growth kinetics and thermal expansion build interfacial stresses.
Interfacial stresses generated in multiphase alloys cause oxide cracking and spallation.
Above 900 °C, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys will develop and maintain a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer.
Under identical high-temperature exposure, multiphase CrFeCoNiX samples will crack and spall more frequently than single-phase samples.
Weight gain is an indirect measure of oxidation kinetics.
The oxide chemistry and stability effects of Si, Mn, and Al may vary with atmospheric conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts the test to CrFeCoNiX compositions, but one proposed baseline is CrFeCoNi without X, which lies outside that stated compositional boundary.
